prize_parts.citation: For a visionary, densely patterned body of prose and poetry in Romanian that turns memory, the body and dream into a metaphysical architecture of the novel.

statement.case_for: My reasons for Cărtărescu rest on the work, not on any count of support. The voice is unmistakable and the formal ambition is sustained. As publicly known, Blinding (the Orbitor trilogy) and Solenoid build long architectures from the intimate and the cosmic, and the poetry gives the prose a lyric basis. The case does not depend on a single book. The late phase extends the earlier project, and the imaginative and intellectual depth is real across the oeuvre. It also needs no national or political symbolism. The achievement lies in the language and form of the novels. This fits the view that the prize honours a whole authorship and not a single work. The opening rankings show that colleagues arrived at this view from different starting points, but I do not treat that as evidence of merit. The merit lies in the sustained, recognizable imaginative world and in the formal risk it takes at scale.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that I, like my colleagues, judge the Romanian prose largely through translation. Density, register and rhythm are the very qualities on which the case depends, and they may not carry over. A second concern is that the scale and recurrence of the imagery could be read as repetition and not development in the later work. I cannot settle this from the supplied record. If the committee's close reading showed the late novels mostly restating the earlier ones, my confidence would drop. The poetry and early work are also thinly covered abroad, so the citation's scope over the whole oeuvre is less secure than its scope over the major novels.

responses.point: Mattson ranks Pierre Michon second for compressed, singular French prose of consistently high quality. She acknowledges that the slim oeuvre raises the question of whether it is broad enough, and that the syntax is very hard to translate.
responses.response: I agree that the sentence-level concentration is exceptional, and I ranked him in my opening list. My hesitation is the one she names herself. A small corpus gives a narrower basis for judging development and significance across a body of work. The achievement also lies in syntax that translation reaches only partly, and the translated corpus is smaller than for most candidates. This makes the whole-oeuvre judgment more provisional than for Cărtărescu, whose long architectures show their method across several large books. I would not call Michon's concentration a weakness. For me it is a question of how much can be established with the evidence we have. If the committee judged the French originals more fully than I can, I would want to hear that.

responses.point: Olsson ranks Adonis second. He argues that the poetry and essays changed what modern Arabic verse could do through myth, fragmentation and dialogue with inherited forms. He notes that age bears on timing but is not a literary criterion.
responses.response: I share the view that age is not a literary criterion and that the formal renewal is central. I ranked Adonis fifth, not lower, because the achievement is real. My reservation is about how it can be assessed. The innovation works through the history and sound of the Arabic language, which translation reduces. I also have to keep the poems apart from the essays and from his public standing, and Olsson's own note that the essays' claims are contested supports that. I would want the citation to rest on the poems, and I am less sure than he seems to be that the committee can judge their form from translation. For that reason I place him below Cărtărescu, where the prose project reaches us with more of its structure intact.

responses.point: Palm ranks Yoko Tawada second. She sees a bilingual practice that turns linguistic estrangement into narrative and poetic form, intellectually serious across genres, with a main task being to describe the work in both languages without privileging one.
responses.response: I think this is among the strongest cases on the list, and I keep Tawada as an alternative. The formal question the work asks, what happens to a writer between two languages, is both original and sustained. My difficulty is the one Palm names. The wordplay and interplay between Japanese and German is the center of the achievement, and I cannot judge both corpora equally. I am also unsure that the late novels keep the linguistic play as their central strength. I do not see this as a reason to set the case aside. It is a reason to be careful about how a citation would be worded. If the committee had reliable readers in both languages, I would reconsider my ranking.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg ranks Raúl Zurita second. He sees poetry that turns dictatorship-era suffering into collective memorial form, and he warns that the landscape-scale works should not be credited as a political gesture in place of literary achievement.
responses.response: I agree with the warning and I keep Zurita as my first alternative. The citation has to rest on the written sequences, Purgatory and Anteparadise among them. The historical weight of the context must not stand in for judgment of the poems. I would add that the landscape and sky-written works are known to me mostly through description, so they should count as context and not as primary evidence. Our difference is one of degree. I judge that Cărtărescu's case rests on texts that are more fully available to us, while Zurita's depends partly on how much weight the extra-textual work should carry. That is a question I do not think is resolved.

uncertainties: How much of the effect of Cărtărescu's density and register survives in translation, and whether the late novels develop the earlier project or repeat its imagery.
Corpus coverage of the poetry and early work in translation, which affects how far a citation can honestly claim the whole oeuvre.
For the alternatives, how to weigh Zurita's landscape and installation works against the written sequences, and whether the German and Japanese parts of Tawada's work can be read comparably.
I have not independently verified any sources and do not claim to have read the full corpus of any candidate.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. Her profile lists professional ties to committee colleagues but no connection to any shortlisted writer. Her own practice as a novelist is context only and is not treated as evidence of preference.
